title: Like the full moon
hook: Punna is told to fill herself with good things, like the moon on the fifteenth night (Therigatha, Punna)
carry: a little more light each evening

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nun with no name, told to rest in the robe she made. Your line was herbs dried in a pot. Did you lay a hand on something you made and let the day finish? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

A thin curve of light low in the evening sky. The next night, a little wider. Then wider again. Nothing is bolted onto the moon. Night by night, more of its face catches the light, until one night the whole round face is lit. A short poem in the Therigatha is built on that picture, and it's spoken to a nun named Punna. Yesterday's poem pictured freedom as something drying out. Today's pictures it as something filling up. Today, like the full moon.
screen: `A THIN CURVE OF LIGHT.` → `WIDER, NIGHT BY NIGHT.` → `THE WHOLE FACE LIT.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Some readers hear a play on it: in Pali, Punna sounds like the word for full. On that hearing, a woman called full is told how to become full. Second, the filling. The poem tells her to fill herself with good things, the good qualities of the teaching. Here the picture is of a vessel being filled. Third, the moon. She is to fill herself like the moon on the fifteenth night, the night it comes full. The moon doesn't get there by force. It gets there a night at a time, a little more light each evening. Fourth, the darkness. With wisdom made full, the poem says, she will tear through the great mass of darkness. A full moon lights a whole field at night, so you can see the path in front of you. That's what the poem promises wisdom does. Put the two poems side by side, yesterday's and today's. Herbs drying in a pot. A moon filling night by night. One is about what goes out of a person, the craving losing its sap. The other is about what comes in, good qualities, growing steadily. The Therigatha holds both pictures without choosing between them. Some teachers call letting go and filling up two sides of one path. And the full-moon nights had a place in the early sangha too: they were observance days, uposatha, when the community gathered.
screen: `A NAME THAT SOUNDS LIKE FULL.` · `FILL YOURSELF WITH GOOD THINGS.` · `LIKE THE MOON ON THE FIFTEENTH.` · `WISDOM TEARS THE DARKNESS.` · then, large: `LIKE THE FULL MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fill the day with one good thing. Settle, and let the breath come and go. Choose one good thing you can add before tonight. Small is fine: a kind message, a short walk outside, a meal made with care, a page of something worth reading. See where it fits: the hour, the place. Not a whole full moon today. Just one night's more light. Then let the choice rest, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Punna. The nun told to fill herself with good things the way the moon fills, until wisdom breaks through the dark. Today's word.
Your line: a little more light each evening. Today, add the one good thing you chose, and tonight, if the sky is clear, look for the moon, whatever shape it's in. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: In Theravada communities the full-moon day is an observance day, uposatha, when lay Buddhists may visit the temple, take extra precepts and listen to teaching, and verses like Punna's are read as pictures of gradual growth on the path.

it compares her to the moon on the fifteenth night, filling up until it's full.

fork.setup: you're Punna. a voice tells you how to grow free. which picture does it give you?
options: empty yourself, like a bowl turned over.
fill yourself with good things, like the moon on the fifteenth night.
burn bright, like a fire on a hill.
fork.reveal: fill yourself with good things, like the full moon, and with wisdom made full, tear through the darkness.

original.note: Pali: the nun's name, Puṇṇā; puṇṇa is the Pali word for full.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty moon image.
what it means: a nun told to grow full of good things, night by night, until wisdom breaks the dark.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear a play on her name, which sounds like the Pali word for full; full-moon days were also uposatha, observance days, in the early sangha.
recall: takes the rules like a garland

notes: Thig 1.3 paraphrased: 'Punna, fill yourself with good qualities like the moon on the fifteenth; with full wisdom, tear apart the mass of darkness.' Confirm, and confirm the verse number.
The wordplay Punna / punna (full) is stated as 'sounds like ... seems to play on it'; confirm it is fair to call it wordplay.
'Other poems speak that way' (emptying) refers loosely to images of letting go elsewhere in the collection; confirm the contrast is fair and not overdrawn.
Uposatha on full-moon days: Mahavagga 2 sets the observance on the fourteenth or fifteenth and the eighth of the fortnight; the script says only that full-moon nights were observance days. Confirm.
howItsDone describes common Theravada lay practice on uposatha days; 'may visit' keeps it non-universal.

Editor pass: name wordplay (Punna/full) now attributed to 'some readers' rather than stated as the name's meaning; cut vague 'other poems speak that way'; 'two sides of the same path' attributed to some teachers.
